idiom.note: function-based behaviors, stateful_actor for the cached peer, bare uint64_t on the hot path, one handshake outside the window

caveats: CAF's scheduler is a work-stealing pool. 'cores' is a thread BUDGET; the workers are pinned one per CPU via caf::thread_hook so the CPU set matches qb's exactly, but CAF still steals across them, which qb's actors cannot do. That is an architectural difference, and it cuts both ways: stealing costs on a two-actor ping-pong and pays on an unbalanced fan-out

wait=1 and wait=0 are the SAME configuration for CAF on this benchmark -- its shipped defaults (aggressive-poll-attempts=100, steal-interval=10). The sweep in docs/TUNING.md section 1 recorded slower results for the more aggressive profiles it compared. Those results do not count steals or prove that no message crossed a core. The caf-detached row measures an explicit worker per actor

in the work-stealing pool the receiver of a message sent from a worker is prepended to that worker's own queue (worker::delay), favouring the sender's worker. Another worker may steal it, so the two-core row does not guarantee same-core hand-offs; caf-detached uses explicit per-actor placement
QVO requests C++20. CAF declares C++17 as a minimum, not a separate compiler mode; the library compilation command is the authority for its effective language mode
